manuscript.title: Whale Optimization Algorithm and Moth-Flame Optimization for Multilevel Thresholding Image Segmentation
manuscript.abstract_text: Determining the optimal thresholding for image segmentation has got more attention in re- cent years since it has many applications. There are several methods used to ﬁnd the optimal thresholding values such as Otsu and Kapur based methods. These methods are suitable for bi-level thresholding case and they can be easily extended to the multilevel case, however, the process of determining the optimal thresholds in the case of multilevel thresholding is time- consuming. To avoid this problem, this paper examines the ability of two nature inspired algorithms namely: Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) and Moth-Flame Optimization (MFO) to determine the optimal multilevel thresholding for image segmentation. The MFO algorithm is inspired from the natural behavior of moths which have a special navigation style at night since they ﬂy using the moonlight, whereas, the WOA algorithm emulates the natural cooperative behaviors of whales. The candidate solutions in the adapted algorithms were created using the image histogram, and then they were updated based on the character- istics of each algorithm. The solutions are assessed using the Otsu’s ﬁtness function during the optimization operation. The performance of the proposed algorithms has been evaluated using several of benchmark images and has been compared with ﬁve diﬀerent swarm algo- rithms. The results have been analyzed based on the best ﬁtness values, PSNR, and SSIM measures, as well as time complexity and the ANOVA test. The experimental results showed that the proposed methods outperformed the other swarm algorithms; in addition, the MFO showed better results than WOA, as well as provided a good balance between exploration and exploitation in all images at small and high threshold numbers.

Abstract
Determining the optimal thresholding for image segmentation has got more attention in re-
cent years since it has many applications. There are several methods used to ﬁnd the optimal
thresholding values such as Otsu and Kapur based methods. These methods are suitable for
bi-level thresholding case and they can be easily extended to the multilevel case, however, the
process of determining the optimal thresholds in the case of multilevel thresholding is time-
consuming. To avoid this problem, this paper examines the ability of two nature inspired
algorithms namely: Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) and Moth-Flame Optimization
(MFO) to determine the optimal multilevel thresholding for image segmentation. The MFO
algorithm is inspired from the natural behavior of moths which have a special navigation
style at night since they ﬂy using the moonlight, whereas, the WOA algorithm emulates the
natural cooperative behaviors of whales. The candidate solutions in the adapted algorithms
were created using the image histogram, and then they were updated based on the character-
istics of each algorithm. The solutions are assessed using the Otsu’s ﬁtness function during
the optimization operation. The performance of the proposed algorithms has been evaluated
using several of benchmark images and has been compared with ﬁve diﬀerent swarm algo-
rithms. The results have been analyzed based on the best ﬁtness values, PSNR, and SSIM
measures, as well as time complexity and the ANOVA test. The experimental results showed
that the proposed methods outperformed the other swarm algorithms; in addition, the MFO
showed better results than WOA, as well as provided a good balance between exploration
and exploitation in all images at small and high threshold numbers.

1. Introduction
Thresholding is one of the popular techniques in image segmentation. It has two cat-
egories: bi-level and multilevel (Sarkar et al., 2013) (Bhandari et al., 2014). The bi-level
thresholding splits the image into two classes, whereas multilevel is used to segment complex
images and it can produce multiple thresholds such as tri-level or quad-level, which split
pixels into multiple similar parts based on intensity (Guo & Li, 2007) (Zhang & Wu, 2011).
Bi-level thresholding can produce adequate outcomes in the case that the image contains
only two principal gray levels, but the foremost restriction is the time-consuming computa-
tion which is often high when it is extended to multilevel thresholding (Dirami et al., 2013).
Basically, two approaches namely parametric and nonparametric (Hammouche et al.,
2008) are used to determine the optimal thresholds. In the ﬁrst one, some statistical pa-
rameters (e.g. time-consuming, and their accuracy) should be computed for the classes in
the image. In the second one, the optimal thresholds are determined by maximizing some
criteria such as the Otsu’ criterion (Otsu, 1979) and Kapur’s entropy (Kapur et al., 1985).
In the Otsu-based method, the best threshold is the one that maximizes the between-class
variance of the regions. Kapur’s entropy measures the homogeneity of the classes by using
the maximization of the entropy. So, the selection of optimal thresholds in multilevel is a
NP-hard problem (Marciniak et al., 2014), and it has been considered as a challenge over
decades (Sarkar et al., 2013; Dirami et al., 2013). When the threshold number is small,
classical techniques are suitable; but if this number increases, the accuracy of segmentation
will be aﬀected. Therefore, to avoid this weakness, many swarm intelligence (SI) techniques
have been applied and combined with thresholding algorithms; such as Genetic Algorithm
(GA) (Elsayed et al., 2014), Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) (J. Kennedy, 1995), Ant
Colony Optimization (ACO) (Kaveh & Talatahari, 2010), Fireﬂy Algorithm (FA) (Yang,
2009), and Social Spider Optimization (SSO) (Cuevas et al., 2013). For example, Pruthi,
J. et al. (Pruthi & Gupta, 2016) presented an algorithm based on GA and its combination
with Otsu to overcome segmentation drawbacks.
Also, PSO is applied to determine the
multilevel thresholding for image segmentation (Ghamisi et al., 2012; Ye et al., 2011). Naik,
P. et al. (Naik & Gopal, 2016) used PSO as a preprocessing technique prior to the image
segmentation. The image is preprocessed to get the optimum pixels and then k-means clus-
tering is applied on the image for segmentation. Whereas, Erdmann, et al. (Erdmann et al.,
2015) presented a ﬁreﬂy algorithm (FA) method for multilevel thresholding segmentation,
and the improved FA (IFA) is used to enhance the performance of FA to solve a multilevel
image thresholding problem as in (Chen et al., 2016). The IFA used Cauchy mutation and
neighborhood strategy to increase the global search ability and accelerate the convergence.
IFA also is utilized to search for multilevel global best thresholds and segment images into
background and objects (Horng, 2011). In addition, Fayad, H. et al. (Fayad et al., 2015)
developed and validated an image segmentation approach based on ACO algorithm. On
the other hand, Agarwal, P., et al.
(Agarwal et al., 2016) deployed histogram based on
bi-modal and multi-modal thresholding for a gray image using SSO. They employed SSO to
maximize Kapur’s and Otsu’s functions values. Furthermore, there are many other swarm
algorithms, that were used for image segmentation including: bacterial foraging algorithm
(BFO) (Bakhshali & Shamsi, 2014) (Sanyal et al., 2011), honey bee mating optimization

(HBMO) (Horng, 2010), wind driven optimization (WDO) (Bayraktar et al., 2013), cuckoo
search (CS) (Agrawal et al., 2013), artiﬁcial bee colony (ABC) (Akay, 2013; Bhandari et al.,
2015), harmony search (HS) algorithm (Oliva et al., 2013), and hybrid swarm (FASSO) (Abd
El-Aziz et al., 2016). However, most of these algorithms have slow convergences to the global
optimal solution (i.e. can get stuck in local optimal) and the quality of segmentation becomes
poor when the number of thresholds is increased. In addition, before applying them, their
parameters must be ﬁne-tuned.
Recently, two new swarm algorithms namely, the whale optimization algorithm (WOA) and
the moth-ﬂame optimization (MFO) are introduced. The WOA is introduced by Mirjalili
in 2016 (Mirjalili & Lewis, 2016) to solve the global optimization problem by emulating the
behavior of humpback whales. The humpback whales have a unique hunting method called
bubble-net feeding (Mirjalili & Lewis, 2016). This behavior works in three diﬀerent phases,
namely, coral loop, lobtail, and capture loop (Mirjalili & Lewis, 2016). More information
about this behavior can be found in (Goldbogen et al., 2013).
The WOA has been used in several applications such as in (Kaveh & Ghazaan, 2016),
(Cherukuri & Rayapudi, 2016), and (J.Touma, 2016), these studies have showed that the
WOA algorithm gives a better accuracy when it is compared to other state-of-the-art evo-
lutionary algorithms such PSO and GA. WOA includes exploration and two approaches of
exploitation that make it be ﬂexible and gradient-free mechanism as well as it has an ability
to avoid local optima and get the global optimal solution that makes it suitable for real
applications. In addition, it does not need structural adjustments in the algorithm for solv-
ing diﬀerent optimization problems because it has only two main parameters to be adapted
(Mirjalili & Lewis, 2016).
On the other hand, Mirjalili (Mirjalili, 2015) had presented MFO, it is a new metaheuristic
algorithm based on the behavior of the moths. Moths have special navigation style at night
since they ﬂy using the moonlight. The moth in nature ﬂies by calculating a ﬁxed angle with
respect to the moon and eventually converges towards the light which makes moths ﬂy in a
straight line; but when there is an artiﬁcial light, the moths ﬂy spirally around the light, since
this light is very close compared to the moon (Mirjalili, 2015). The power of MFO algorithm
is appeared by increasing exploration of the search space and decreasing the possibility of
being trapped in local optima, since it assigns each moth a ﬂame and updates the series
of ﬂames in every iteration, as well as, saves the best-obtained position in ﬂames so they
never get lost and works as guides for the moths (Mirjalili, 2015). In (Mirjalili, 2015), (Li
et al., 2016), (Nanda et al., 2016), and (Parmar et al., 2016), the MFO was compared with
other swarm algorithms to solve several continuous and discrete optimization problems. Its
results proved high exploitation capability, applicability to solve real problems, and ability
to optimize search spaces with infeasible regions.
To sum up, these algorithms have many advantages such as: having a small number of
parameters, simple frameworks, and ability to avoid the problem of getting stuck in the local
optima. Therefore, they can be suitable for many real applications and can solve several
global optimization problems without changing the structure of the original algorithm. In
addition, both MFO and WOA algorithms have operators to balance between exploration
and exploitation, unlike other optimizations (e.g. PSO and GA) they apply one equation
to update the agent’s position, which can increase the trapping probability in local optima.

Based on the success of both the proposed algorithms (WOA and MFO) in several applica-
tions, this study further illustrates their power to solve image segmentation problems using
multilevel thresholding. The Otsu’s criterion is used as a ﬁtness function to assess the solu-
tions in each population of the two algorithms and then determine the best accuracy of the
segmented images. In addition, MFO and WOA algorithms tune their control parameters
through searching for the global solution which avoids the problem of pre-deﬁned control
parameters that can be unsuitable for solving the problem.
The main contributions of this study are two-fold: (1) introduce Whale Optimization
Algorithm (WOA) and the Moth-Flame Optimization (MFO) algorithms for selecting an
optimal threshold value. (2) Compare between WOA and MFO in such context. To the best
of our knowledge, this concept has not been investigated yet.
The two proposed algorithms generate random solutions in domain bounded by the image
histogram. During the updating process, the quality of each solution is evaluated using the
between-class variance function. According to the ﬁtness function value, the set of solutions
is updated based on the characteristics of the WOA and MFO until a termination criterion
is satisﬁed. The results of the WOA and MFO algorithms have been compared with other
metaheuristic algorithms. The performance of the diﬀerent algorithms has been assessed
on various images using the best ﬁtness values and two other criteria namely: the peak-to-
signal-noise ratio (PSNR) and the structural similarity index (SSIM), as well as the time
complexity which is taken into account; in addition, the analysis of variance between all the
algorithms has been tested using an ANOVA test.
The rest of this paper is arranged as follows: in Section 2, the problem formulation and the
deﬁnition of Otsu’s method are introduced. The proposed algorithms for multilevel thresh-
olding based on WOA and MFO algorithms are illustrated in Section 3. The experiments
and results are given in Section 4. Finally, the conclusion and future work are listed in the
last section.

multilevel thresholding for image segmentation that maximizes the Otsu’s objective function.

4. Experiments and Results
In this section, we introduce the environment of the experiments for the proposed al-
gorithms. The description of benchmark images is introduced ﬁrstly, then the parameters
setting for each algorithm are illustrated brieﬂy and a set of quality metrics are used to
evaluate the quality of the segmentation process.
4.1. Benchmark images
In this paper, the proposed algorithms are tested on eight common grayscale images from
the database of Berkeley University (Martin et al., 2001). These images are called, TestE4,
TestE1, Test1, Test6, Test5, Test11, Test3, and Test9 as illustrated in Figure 3.

works and proved good results. For a fair comparison, all algorithms used in this paper have

thresholding for image segmentation has been considered as an optimization problem where

algorithm is to determine the best thresholds value that maximizes the Otsu’s function.
